issues.legal_issue: A payment received by a lessor under a lease covenant is taxable income to the extent it exceeds the lessor’s actual liability for the public cess being reimbursed.
material_facts: A mining lease required the lessee to pay public demands relating to the mines, apart from land revenue.

The lessee paid the lessor sums described as local fund cess, calculated by reference to rent and royalties, although the cess legally payable was calculated by reference to land revenue and was substantially lower.
The lessor received and appropriated the payments as if entitled to them.
issues.conclusion: The excess of the sums received over the reimbursement the lessor could claim for the cess was income and, absent a specific exemption, was taxable.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(6C) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, income is inclusively defined; anything properly described as income is taxable unless expressly exempted. The Court relied on Gopal Saran Narain Singh v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bihar & Orissa, and held that payments under a covenant directly related to rent and royalty, having a quality closely similar to rent and royalty, are income when received and appropriated by the lessor.

predicates.income_tax_assessment: The dispute arises in an income-tax assessment proceeding.
predicates.lease_requires_lessee_to_pay_public_dema: A lease requires the lessee to pay or reimburse public demands relating to the leased property.
predicates.lessee_paid_lessor_more_than_actual_cess: The lessee paid the lessor more for a public charge than the lessor was actually liable to pay for that charge.
predicates.lessor_received_payment_as_entitled: The lessor received and appropriated the payment as a receipt to which the lessor was entitled.

issues.definition: When an income-tax assessment concerns an excess payment made under a lease covenant and the lessor receives it as entitled, the excess is treated as taxable income.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee’s contractual payment to reimburse a landholder’s statutory liability does not make the lessee an inferior holder or make the landholder an agent collecting the charge for the government.
material_facts: The landholder held the land and granted the mining lease to the lessee.
The applicable land-revenue law imposed liability for land revenue and local fund cess on the landholder, and no provision was identified that imposed that cess liability on the lessee as a lessee.
The lease required the lessee to pay public demands, so the lessee agreed to reimburse the landholder for the charge the landholder owed.
The landholder collected the payment under the lease and did not purport to collect the cess on behalf of the government.
issues.conclusion: The lessee was not an inferior holder; the landholder remained liable for the cess, and the landholder was not the government’s agent for collecting it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied sections 3(13), 3(14) and 45 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, concerning superior holders, tenants and liability for land revenue, together with sections 93 and 96 of the Bombay Local Boards Act, 1923, concerning local fund cess. The contractual promise to reimburse the landholder did not transfer the statutory liability to the lessee or create an agency relationship with the government.

rule.if: lease_and_cess_dispute and landholder_holds_land and law_places_cess_liability_on_landholder and lessee_promised_reimbursement

predicates.lease_and_cess_dispute: The proceeding concerns a lease and a disputed payment or liability for a public cess.
predicates.landholder_holds_land: The person granting the lease holds the land to which the statutory charge relates.
predicates.law_places_cess_liability_on_landholder: The applicable law places liability for the charge on the landholder rather than on the lessee merely as lessee.
predicates.lessee_promised_reimbursement: The lease requires the lessee to pay or reimburse the landholder for the public charge.

issues.definition: If a landholder is legally liable for a charge and a lessee has only promised to reimburse it under the lease, the lessee is not treated as an inferior holder and the landholder is not treated as a government collection agent.

issues.legal_issue: An income-tax authority may determine the amount of a statutory charge relevant to an assessment even if that determination does not bind another person or body.
material_facts: The amount of local fund cess legally payable by the landholder was relevant to determining how much of the lessee’s payment was reimbursement and how much was excess income.
The issue arose in proceedings assessing the landholder’s income.
The Court found no provision preventing the revenue authorities from determining the landholder’s cess liability for assessment purposes.
issues.conclusion: The income-tax authority could determine the amount of cess payable by the landholder when that question properly arose in the assessment.
issues.legal_principle: The Income-tax Act, 1922 assigns the assessing authority jurisdiction to determine whether a receipt is income and taxable as between the State and the assessee. The authority is not prevented from deciding a relevant question merely because its determination may not bind another person or body.

predicates.income_tax_assessment: The dispute arises in an income-tax assessment proceeding.
predicates.charge_amount_relevant_to_assessment: The amount of a statutory charge affects whether or how much of a receipt is income in the assessment.
predicates.charge_amount_question_properly_arises: The question of the charge’s amount properly arises for decision in the assessment proceeding.

issues.definition: When the amount of a statutory charge is relevant and properly arises in an income-tax assessment, the assessing authority may determine it for that assessment.

issues.legal_issue: Executive accounting instructions cannot change the statutory basis on which a public cess is levied.
material_facts: The governing statute required the local fund cess to be levied by reference to land revenue.
The landholder relied on a government revenue-account manual that listed rent and royalties under mining leases among accounting entries associated with local fund revenue.
The Court treated the manual’s directions as instructions about accounting entries, not as a change to the statutory basis for levying the cess.
issues.conclusion: The manual did not make rent and royalties the statutory basis for calculating the cess; executive instructions could not modify the statute.
issues.legal_principle: The Bombay Local Boards Act, 1923, including sections 93 and 96, prescribed the basis and manner of levying the cess. Executive instructions concerning revenue-account entries cannot amend or override those statutory requirements.

predicates.cess_calculation_dispute: The proceeding concerns the basis for calculating a statutory cess.
predicates.statute_prescribes_charge_basis: A statute prescribes the basis on which the charge is to be calculated.
predicates.executive_manual_addresses_accounting_en: An executive manual addresses how related receipts or entries are recorded in accounts.

issues.definition: When a statute prescribes the basis for a charge, accounting instructions in an executive manual do not change that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A payer’s later claim to recover a payment does not deprive the payment of its character as income in the year it was received.
material_facts: The landholder received the payment from the lessee under the lease.
The lessee later filed a suit seeking recovery of the excess payment.
The Court was not deciding the merits of the recovery claim.
issues.conclusion: The possibility or pursuit of a refund did not alter the payment’s character as income in the year of receipt.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a receipt which is income when received does not lose that character for the year of receipt merely because the payer may claim or seek a refund.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment and taxpayer_received_payment and payment_is_income_when_received and payer_claims_or_may_claim_refund

predicates.income_tax_assessment: The dispute arises in an income-tax assessment proceeding.
predicates.taxpayer_received_payment: The taxpayer received a payment from another person.
predicates.payment_is_income_when_received: The payment has the character of income when received.
predicates.payer_claims_or_may_claim_refund: The payer may seek, or has sought, repayment of the payment.

issues.definition: If a taxpayer receives a payment that is income when received, a possible or actual refund claim by the payer does not change that character.

issues.legal_issue: A receipt arising from a contractual payment is not exempt as casual and non-recurring merely because the payer may have paid it by mistake.
material_facts: The disputed payments were made under a lease covenant concerning public demands.
Payments were made for two successive periods.

The contention that the receipts were casual and non-recurring had been abandoned before the Tribunal, and the Court found no characteristic of casualness or suggestion that the receipts were non-recurring.
issues.conclusion: The receipts were not exempt as casual and non-recurring.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(vii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 exempted income of a casual and non-recurring nature. The Court held that a receipt is not casual merely because it may have resulted from the payer’s mistake; it must have the characteristic of casualness, and the receipts here were not shown to be non-recurring.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment and receipt_arises_from_contract and receipt_lacks_casual_character and receipt_is_not_shown_to_be_nonrecurring

predicates.income_tax_assessment: The dispute arises in an income-tax assessment proceeding.
predicates.receipt_arises_from_contract: The receipt is made under a contractual arrangement.
predicates.receipt_lacks_casual_character: The receipt is not accidental, fortuitous or from an unforeseen source.
predicates.receipt_is_not_shown_to_be_nonrecurring: The evidence does not show that the receipt is non-recurring.

issues.definition: A contractual receipt that lacks a casual character and is not shown to be non-recurring does not qualify for the casual-and-non-recurring exemption.
